transcript:
>> This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder, a federal judge in California is restricting
Department of Homeland Security field operations in nine states that are trying to find non-citizens
who previously voted.
NPR's Jude Joffe Block reports a ruling cited the Voting Rights Act, which bars voter intimidation.
The Trump administration has been laser focused on finding and arresting non-citizens who
illegally voted.
Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin wrote that effort is using data that appears unreliable.
And she wrote federal officers knocking on doors looking for people based on that data
is intimidating eligible voters.
She also noted federal officials are targeting new citizens who may have voted before naturalizing.
The order blocks federal officers from targeting people known or suspected to be U.S. citizens
or relying on incomplete data without further investigation.
The order is set to take effect Friday and stay in place through election night, though
the federal government could appeal.
Jude Joffe Block, NPR News.
>> President Trump's envoy is calling Russian President Vladimir Putin a humanitarian after
Russia released an American man who was captured by Russia in Ukraine.
And British Michelle Kellerman reports that Trump says he asked Putin to release Stephen
Hubbard, who is now on his way home.
>> President Trump calls it an amazing thing that Hubbard was released, and he says he
gave nothing in exchange.
But the news came soon after Trump made a diesel deal with Russia and waved sanctions,
facing pushback from many in Washington, including Republicans who say Trump should be putting
more pressure on Russia.
>> If we did what these foolish people wanted me to do, he wouldn't be coming out right now.
He'd be in there for another 20 years.
So the last thing I was gonna do is break up that.
>> Hubbard, a retired teacher, was living in eastern Ukraine when Russia invaded and
captured him, accusing him of being a mercenary.
The US considered him a hostage.
Michelle Kellerman, NPR News, the State Department.
>> The state of New Mexico is suing Jeffrey Epstein's former attorney and his former accountant.
The lawsuit filed Wednesday accuses the two men of concealing Epstein's sex trafficking
operations at his ranch near Santa Fe, and it seeks to stop them from profiting from
Epstein's estate, New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torres.
>> People who are a part of a criminal enterprise should not financially benefit from anything
like the $100 million that's left in Jeffrey Epstein's estate.
>> A lawyer for attorney Darren Indike and accountant Richard Kahn says they deny any
knowledge of abuse.
Also in New Mexico, a state judge has ordered tech giant Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion
for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook.
The fine imposed Wednesday is believed to be the biggest ever against Meta, which says
it will appeal.
This is NPR.
The pro-Israel political organization, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee,
also known as APAC, says it will no longer issue endorsements, make direct PAC contributions
or earmark funds for candidates.
NPR's Sage Miller reports that the group also has had bipartisan support and influence
in the past, but its positions and tactics have become more polarizing.
>> APAC started its political involvement five years ago, but the pro-Israel group has
caught a lot of heat this election cycle over its stances on various issues such as the
war in Gaza.
APAC has also become a liability for some candidates endorsed by the group.
They've come under fire on both the right and the left for accepting APAC support and
money.
But APAC isn't going away.
In a letter to members, the group says its Super PAC United Democracy Project will stick
around.
The Super PAC will be able to raise an unlimited amount of money and has spent heavily to support
pro-Israel candidates and oppose those who criticize Israel.
Sage Miller, NPR News.
>> The Trump administration wants to resume building the border wall through Texas' Big
Bend region.
It's asking the Supreme Court to lift a lower court's halt on construction.
The judge in the case ordered construction to stop earlier this month, siding with opponents
who argue that the waivers used to bypass regulations exceed the authority of the Homeland
Security Secretary.
Asian shares retreating and Thursday trading South Korean stocks have declined more than
3%.
I'm Jyle Snyder, this is NPR News.

Trump envoy calls Putin a humanitarian after Russia releases American Stephen Hubbard held in Ukraine
New Mexico sues Jeffrey Epstein's former attorney and accountant over concealed sex trafficking operations
Judge orders Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion for deceiving Facebook users about privacy
AIPAC says it will stop endorsements and direct PAC contributions, while its super PAC continues
Trump administration asks Supreme Court to resume border wall construction through Texas' Big Bend region
South Korean stocks fall more than 3% in Thursday trading as Asian shares retreat
